title: Syntax and Variables
summary: Statements, blocks and comments; declaring variables with int, double, bool, char and string; var and const; string interpolation; arithmetic and console input.
introduction: Every C# program is built from the same few pieces: statements that do one thing each, variables that hold values of a declared type, and expressions that combine them. This lesson covers the syntax you will use in every file from now on: how to declare and name variables, the difference between var and an explicit type, constants, string interpolation, integer versus floating-point arithmetic, and reading a value typed by the user.
learningObjectives: Declare variables with explicit types, var and const
Build strings with interpolation and do arithmetic with the right numeric type
Read input from the console and convert it to a number

blocks.text: A **statement** is one instruction and ends with a semicolon. Line breaks and indentation do not matter to the compiler, so a long statement may span several lines. Curly braces group statements into a **block**, which you will use with `if`, loops, methods and classes. Comments are ignored by the compiler: `//` comments to the end of the line, `/* ... */` can span lines, and `///` starts a documentation comment that editors show as a tooltip.

blocks.text: A variable is a named slot that holds a value of one **type**. You declare it by writing the type, a name and, usually, an initial value. The type is fixed for the life of the variable: an `int` can never hold text, and the compiler enforces that.

blocks.text: The [next lesson](/tutorials/csharp/types) looks at these types in depth. Note the suffixes: `m` makes a literal a `decimal`, `L` makes it a `long`, and `1_000_000` uses digit separators that the compiler ignores. A `bool` prints as `True` or `False` with a capital letter.

items: Names contain letters, digits and underscores and cannot start with a digit. They are case-sensitive: `total` and `Total` are different variables.
Keywords such as `int`, `class` or `if` cannot be used as names.

By convention local variables and parameters use **camelCase** (`orderTotal`), while types, methods and properties use **PascalCase** (`OrderTotal`). Choose names that say what the value *means*, not what type it is.

blocks.text: When the type is obvious from the right-hand side, `var` lets the compiler infer it. The variable is still statically typed: `var city = "Lisbon";` makes `city` a `string` forever. `const` declares a value that can never change and must be known at compile time.

blocks.content:
Lisbon has about 549000 residents.
Two weeks are 14 days.

blocks.text: Use `var` when the type is visible on the same line (a literal, a `new` expression, a cast) and write the type out when it is not, for example for the result of a method call, so readers do not have to guess.

Strings can be joined with `+`, but the readable way to build text is an **interpolated string**: prefix it with `$` and put any expression inside braces. A colon after the expression adds a format, such as `:F2` for two decimal places.

blocks.text: Two other string forms are useful. A **verbatim** string (`@"C:\temp"`) keeps backslashes as they are, which is handy for Windows paths. A **raw string literal** (C# 11 and later) starts and ends with three double quotes and may contain quotes and line breaks without escaping, which is perfect for JSON or SQL snippets. Strings are immutable: `ToUpper()` returns a new string and leaves `first` unchanged.

C# has the usual operators `+ - * / %` plus `++`, `--` and compound forms such as `+=`. One rule surprises everyone once: dividing two integers produces an integer, with the remainder thrown away. Convert one operand to `double` when you want a fraction, and use `%` to get the remainder itself.
`Math` is a static class with `Max`, `Min`, `Abs`, `Pow`, `Sqrt`, `Round` and more. Mixing an `int` with a `double`, as in the last line, promotes the result to `double`.

`Console.ReadLine()` returns what the user typed as a `string`, or `null` if the input stream has ended, which is why its declared type is `string?`. To treat the text as a number, convert it with `int.Parse` or `double.Parse`; the next lesson introduces `TryParse` for input that may be invalid.
Numbers are printed using your machine's regional settings: on a computer set to German, the same program prints `37,50`. The outputs in this tutorial assume English settings.

blocks.title: Unassigned variables
blocks.text: A local variable must be given a value before it is read. `int count; Console.WriteLine(count);` is rejected with *error CS0165: Use of unassigned local variable 'count'*. The same strictness applies to types: `int total = "5";` fails with *CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'int'*, which is exactly the kind of bug static typing exists to catch.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Both operands are integers, so `9 / 2` is `4` (the fraction is dropped) and `9 % 2` is the remainder `1`. Their sum is `5`.

questions.question: `var total = 10;` creates a variable whose type can later change, for example to a string.
questions.explanation: `var` only asks the compiler to infer the type from the initial value. `total` is an `int` for its whole life; assigning a string to it is a compile error.
